fields.label: Description
fields.value: A detailed machine-readable graph of BitTorrent protocol architecture, participants, torrent metadata, integrity mechanisms, peer discovery, transfer algorithms, publishing and search, privacy/security, implementations, history, legal distinctions, adoption examples, and technical relationships. Claims are grounded primarily in the supplied article text; historical statistics remain time-bounded.

notes: The supplied article is the basis for article-derived factual claims.
Some relationship descriptions are normalized explanations of mechanisms explicitly described in the article.
The graph distinguishes protocol integrity from content safety and legal authorization.
Historical adoption statistics and malware-study figures are retained as historical claims, not current estimates.

value.name: Publish content and join a BitTorrent swarm
value.summary: A publisher creates torrent metadata, publishes a .torrent file or magnet link, seeds the complete content, and clients discover peers and exchange verified pieces.

steps.action: Prepare the files and choose piece length and metadata parameters.
Generate torrent metadata and piece hashes; v1 uses SHA-1 and v2 uses SHA-256/Merkle-tree structures.
Publish the .torrent file or magnet link through an index or another distribution channel.
Make a complete copy available so initial downloaders can obtain pieces.
Discover peers through trackers, DHT, and/or peer exchange.
Exchange pieces with peers; verify received pieces against metadata hashes.
Reassemble verified pieces into the file and optionally continue seeding.

value.name: Peer discovery with tracker, DHT, and PEX
value.summary: Peer discovery can combine centralized trackers, decentralized DHT lookup, and peer exchange. These mechanisms are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

steps.action: Read tracker endpoints from torrent metadata when present.
Ask tracker services for peers, if reachable.
Join the DHT via a bootstrap server and look up peers when DHT is enabled.
Exchange peer information with connected peers using PEX when supported.
Connect to candidate peers and repeat discovery as peer membership changes.

value.name: BitTorrent v2 integrity verification and hybrid compatibility
value.summary: BitTorrent v2 uses SHA-256 and Merkle-tree-based hashes for finer-grained integrity checks. Hybrid metadata includes v1 and v2 hashes to support older and newer clients.

steps.action: Hash content at file and piece granularity using the v2 format.
Obtain the torrent metadata or equivalent magnet metadata.
Transfer pieces from one or more peers or web seeds.
Verify the received content against the expected hash tree.
For hybrid torrents, use the included v1/v2 metadata to interoperate with compatible legacy and v2 clients.

value.name: Piece selection and reciprocal uploading
value.summary: A client selects available pieces, prioritizes rare pieces to preserve diversity, and uses choking/unchoking policies plus optimistic unchoking to manage upload partners.

steps.action: Track missing pieces and the pieces advertised by connected peers.
Prefer rare pieces to reduce the chance that a piece disappears from the swarm.
Use choking/unchoking decisions to allocate upload bandwidth.
Use optimistic unchoking to try a peer that may become a better exchange partner and help newcomers acquire initial pieces.
Verify and share successfully received pieces, increasing swarm capacity.

value.name: Hybrid peer and web-seed distribution
value.summary: A publisher can combine conventional HTTP/FTP hosting with peer-to-peer delivery, using the web server as an initial or fallback source while the swarm takes on increasing load.

steps.action: Host the content on a web server and publish torrent metadata.
Obtain pieces from the web seed and from peers where available.
Upload received pieces to other peers.
Optionally reduce or stop direct web serving when the swarm has enough seeders.

value.name: BitTorrent privacy and trust boundaries
value.summary: The base protocol exposes peer IP addresses and does not provide anonymity. VPNs, seedboxes, Tor-like systems, or I2P change the trust and visibility model but introduce their own constraints.

steps.action: Connect to swarm peers; peer endpoints may be visible to other participants.
If using a VPN or seedbox, recognize that the intermediary can observe some user activity or network metadata.
If using Tor-like routing, consider client compatibility and network impact; the article cautions that most clients are not designed for safe torrenting over Tor.
Treat downloaded payloads as untrusted and verify integrity; a valid hash proves correspondence to metadata, not that the content is benign or legally authorized.

value.name: Swarm availability failure and recovery
value.summary: A swarm can lose availability when all complete seeds disappear. Multiple discovery paths do not solve missing-content availability; durable seeds, bundling, or cross-torrent strategies can help.

steps.action: Download pieces and optionally seed them after completion.
Remain online to provide a complete source for missing pieces.
If no complete seed remains and required pieces are missing, the download may stall indefinitely.
Improve long-term availability by maintaining seeds, bundling related content, or using proposed cross-torrent cooperation.

value.title: The BitTorrent Protocol Specification (v1)
value.scope_note: Protocol baseline; cited by the supplied article for core protocol and torrent metadata.

value.title: The BitTorrent Protocol Specification v2
value.scope_note: The article describes SHA-256, Merkle-tree-based verification, per-file hashing, hybrid compatibility, and v2 magnet-link support.

value.title: DHT Protocol
value.scope_note: Mainline DHT peer-discovery mechanism described in the article as Kademlia-based.

value.title: Peer Exchange (PEX)
value.scope_note: Peer Exchange mechanism for discovering additional peers from already connected peers.

value.title: WebSeed — HTTP/FTP Seeding
value.scope_note: HTTP/FTP source integration for downloading torrent pieces.

value.title: Measuring Large-Scale Distributed Systems: Case of BitTorrent Mainline DHT
value.scope_note: Historical measurement reference for Mainline DHT scale and churn.

value.title: P2P File-Sharing in Hell: Exploiting BitTorrent Vulnerabilities to Launch Distributed Reflective DoS Attacks
value.scope_note: Security research cited by the article concerning UDP-based amplification/reflection risks.

value.core_mechanism: Content is divided into pieces. Clients discover peers using trackers, DHT, and/or PEX; exchange pieces across many connections; verify pieces using hashes; reassemble files; and can continue uploading pieces to other peers.
key_architecture_tradeoffs: Distribution capacity can grow as peers join, but a swarm still needs sufficient seeders and piece availability.
Trackers are straightforward but add a centralized discovery dependency; DHT and PEX provide alternative discovery paths.
Rarest-first improves piece diversity, while non-sequential downloading can complicate streaming playback.
v2 improves hashing and granular integrity verification; hybrid torrents preserve compatibility with v1-only clients.
The base protocol does not provide anonymity; privacy overlays change who can observe network endpoints and add trust or performance tradeoffs.
Cryptographic integrity does not establish that content is benign or legally authorized.
important_distinctions: Torrent metadata and indexes are discovery artifacts; the payload is transferred between peers.
A tracker coordinates peer discovery; it is not ordinarily the source of the file bytes.
A seed has the complete content; a downloading peer may have only some pieces.
DHT peer discovery does not itself guarantee that any peer still has the missing pieces.
Protocol legality is distinct from whether a particular distribution is authorized.
Historical traffic and malware statistics in the article should not be interpreted as current universal measurements.

value.expression: C source → machine code → CPU/memory/platform resources

value.description: First edition of The C Programming Language.

value.label: ANSI standardization
value.description: ANSI X3J11 formed and C89 ratified.

value.distinction: C++ adds OO/generic features and stronger typing/scoping to C-like syntax.
Static typing and weak enforcement describe different properties.

value.topic: Pass by value vs reference-like pointers
value.distinction: C passes values; pointers can provide reference-like access.
Arrays are objects; most expressions convert arrays to first-element pointers.

value.topic: Static vs automatic vs dynamic storage

value.distinction: I/O, strings, math and allocation are primarily library facilities.
Portability depends on avoiding platform-specific assumptions.
Null points to no valid location; dangling points to expired storage.
Source contrasts C pointer freedom with Rust safety measures.
Objective-C is a strict C superset with OO and Smalltalk influence.
C indexing normally does not check bounds.
C17 mainly corrected/clarified C11 while C99/C11/C23 added features.
Pointers enable hardware/structures/callbacks but create safety hazards.
C offers portable source-level constructs while retaining low-level control.

value.title: Performance model
value.goal: Why C performs well and where optimization is constrained.

value.correction: C passes parameters by value; pointers provide reference-like access.

value.misconception: An array is just a pointer.
value.correction: Arrays are objects that convert to pointers in most expression contexts.

value.misconception: C has a built-in string type.
value.correction: C uses null-terminated character arrays and library functions.
Dynamic memory normally requires explicit management.

value.misconception: Static typing means strong type safety.
value.correction: The source describes C as statically but weakly typed.
Platform assumptions, libraries, ABI and data layout can reduce portability.

value.misconception: C is only for operating systems.
value.correction: It is also used in embedded, games, servers, libraries and interoperability.
C11 added atomic operations and multithreading.

value.misconception: C and C++ are the same language.
value.correction: C++ is a distinct extension/evolution with additional features.

value.misconception: C is either low-level or portable, not both.
value.correction: C deliberately combines low-level access with portable source semantics.
Pointers support memory, structures, callbacks and hardware access.

value.misconception: The C standard library is the core language.

source_claims.statement: C is a general-purpose language created in 1972 by Dennis Ritchie for relatively direct CPU architecture access.
C is used for operating systems, kernels, drivers, protocol stacks, supercomputers, microcontrollers and embedded systems.
C evolved from B/New B in the context of Unix development and reimplemented the Unix kernel.
C is static, weakly enforced/typed, manifest and nominal.
C provides static, automatic and dynamic storage with manual management.
C combines low-level access with portability through standardized semantics.
The preprocessor provides macros/inclusion/conditional compilation and libraries extend the small core.
Array and pointer semantics are tightly coupled; unchecked bounds are both powerful and risky.
C evolved from K&R through C89/C90/C95/C99/C11/C17/C23 and C2Y/C29.
Embedded C addresses fixed-point arithmetic, named address spaces and hardware I/O.
C is used in systems, games, servers, CGI history and computational libraries.
C interoperates with assembly and higher-level languages and implements other language runtimes.
C has memory, type-safety, runtime-checking, aliasing, ABI, preprocessing and error-handling limitations.
Coding standards, analysis tools and hardware capabilities mitigate subsets of C risks.
C influenced a broad family of programming and hardware-description languages.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: C++ adds OO/generic features and stronger typing/scoping to C-like syntax.
Static typing and weak enforcement describe different properties.

semantic_distinctions.topic: Pass by value vs reference-like pointers
semantic_distinctions.distinction: C passes values; pointers can provide reference-like access.
Arrays are objects; most expressions convert arrays to first-element pointers.

semantic_distinctions.topic: Static vs automatic vs dynamic storage

semantic_distinctions.distinction: I/O, strings, math and allocation are primarily library facilities.
Portability depends on avoiding platform-specific assumptions.
Null points to no valid location; dangling points to expired storage.
Source contrasts C pointer freedom with Rust safety measures.
Objective-C is a strict C superset with OO and Smalltalk influence.
C indexing normally does not check bounds.
C17 mainly corrected/clarified C11 while C99/C11/C23 added features.
Pointers enable hardware/structures/callbacks but create safety hazards.
C offers portable source-level constructs while retaining low-level control.

learning_paths.title: Performance model
learning_paths.goal: Why C performs well and where optimization is constrained.

misconceptions.correction: C passes parameters by value; pointers provide reference-like access.

misconceptions.misconception: An array is just a pointer.
misconceptions.correction: Arrays are objects that convert to pointers in most expression contexts.

misconceptions.misconception: C has a built-in string type.
misconceptions.correction: C uses null-terminated character arrays and library functions.
Dynamic memory normally requires explicit management.

misconceptions.misconception: Static typing means strong type safety.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes C as statically but weakly typed.
Platform assumptions, libraries, ABI and data layout can reduce portability.

misconceptions.misconception: C is only for operating systems.
misconceptions.correction: It is also used in embedded, games, servers, libraries and interoperability.
C11 added atomic operations and multithreading.

misconceptions.misconception: C and C++ are the same language.
misconceptions.correction: C++ is a distinct extension/evolution with additional features.

misconceptions.misconception: C is either low-level or portable, not both.
misconceptions.correction: C deliberately combines low-level access with portable source semantics.
Pointers support memory, structures, callbacks and hardware access.

misconceptions.misconception: The C standard library is the core language.
